description: Hi! We are 2ISI, a team from UNISON, made up of six software engineering students seeking to expand our skills to solve real-world problems.
summary: Signal Lost is a web game, with 100% original hand-drawn art, that trains kids to think like real astronauts. The robot explorers on the Moon and Mars have gone silent, and the player, a young space specialist, must bring them back. Kids repair Pragyan, Curiosity, Phoenix and Opportunity through hands-on minigames while managing four base resources: energy, life support, food and shielding. Every action has a cost, so they learn to plan before they act. On Mars, messages from Sam, their flight director on Earth, arrive late, just like real communications, so kids must make their own decisions. Solar storms and radiation come from real NASA data (DONKI and Curiosity’s RAD detector), and each repaired robot unlocks a real fact about its mission. This answers the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by turning astronaut skills into play: resource planning, step-by-step problem solving, reading space data and working independently. It matters because future explorers will need these skills far from Earth, and the game lets any child start practicing them today, for free, on any laptop, tablet or phone.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
Signal Lost is a mission-based game built in Unity and published for the web with WebGL. Players first pick a difficulty level. Cadet gives extra tips and a crew rescue if things go wrong, and Commander is the real challenge. The journey has three stages:

  1. Moon tutorial: the player fixes Pragyan, whose battery died during the long lunar night. They reconnect its cables and drive the rover. Sam’s messages arrive almost instantly here, because the Moon is only 1.3 light-seconds away.
    • Curiosity: a solar storm put it in safe mode. Players decide whether to shield or wait, then switch it from computer A to computer B, position the arm and mast, and reactivate the antenna.
    • Phoenix: players break the ice that jammed its scoop and unclog its oven grate.
    • Opportunity: players brush dust off its solar panels and restart the reactor.

Each repaired robot gives a lasting upgrade (an early storm warning, more water, more energy) and a robot file with a real fact. On Mars, Sam’s advice arrives late to reflect the 3–22 minute signal delay, so players have to think on their own.

What benefits does it have?
Kids practice real astronaut skills: planning limited resources, solving problems step by step, reading real data and making decisions without help from Earth. Because every action has a cost, choices matter and the lessons stick. They get a free, ready-to-use activity that connects play with real NASA science.

What is the intended impact?
We want kids to feel what it is like to be an astronaut: careful, patient and independent. We also want them to discover the real robots and real data behind space exploration. If a child leaves the game curious about Curiosity’s radiation detector or why Opportunity lasted 15 years, the game did its job.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Coding languages: C# for the game logic; JavaScript for the browser gyroscope bridge and the website; HTML and CSS for the website; PowerShell scripts to download and prepare the NASA data.
  • Software: Unity 6 (URP, Input System, TextMesh Pro), Unity Version Control, Unity WebGL build, Astro and Visual Studio Code for the website, GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting, and Canva for the UI design, Clip Studio Paint and Sketchbook for art.
  • Hardware: developed on Windows laptops. The game is designed for laptops, tablets and phones, and it uses the device’s gyroscope and accelerometer for tilt controls when available.
  • Static Data: NASA DONKI and NASA OSDR RadLab (Curiosity RAD).

How is your project creative?

  • 100% original, hand-drawn art. Every character, robot, background and screen in the game and on the website was drawn by hand by our team. We did not use any AI-generated images or stock art, so Signal Lost has its own visual identity.
  • The silence is the game. The whole story starts with losing contact, and the game turns that into how it plays. On the Moon, Sam answers almost instantly. On Mars, help from Earth arrives late, just like real signals. Instead of a teacher saying “now you’re on your own,” physics does it, and kids slowly learn to trust their own decisions.
  • Real robots get a second chance. Pragyan never woke up after the lunar night, Phoenix froze in the Martian winter, and Opportunity was buried by dust. We took real mission endings and turned them into rescue missions, so kids connect emotionally with real space history instead of just reading about it.
  • Kids play through a real solar storm. The storms in the game aren’t invented: they come from the May 2024 solar storms recorded by NASA, the strongest in about 20 years. Kids face the same space weather that Curiosity faced on Mars.
  • Nothing is free. Most kids’ games reward you for pressing buttons. In Signal Lost, every repair, every move and every sol costs resources, so a good astronaut thinks before acting.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Energy: the website loads the game only when the player presses “Start Mission”, images are compressed (WebP), and everything is hosted as static files, with no servers running in the background. Inside the game, energy is the main resource kids must save.
  • Accessibility: the game works with tilt, touch, mouse or keyboard. It has two difficulty levels, dialog that moves at the player’s own pace, and voice acting for younger readers. On the website, the robot cards include descriptions for screen readers and reduced-motion support.
  • Cost: it is free to play and needs no installation or special hardware. It runs in the browser on devices schools already have, and it was built entirely with free tools and free hosting.
  • Positive feedback: we designed the game so kids always feel they are making progress, not failing. Every repaired robot gives a reward and a mission-complete screen with stars, and Sam celebrates each step. In Cadet mode, if the base runs out of resources, the crew is rescued instead of the game simply ending. In Commander mode, the game explains what went wrong so kids can learn and try again. This keeps them motivated and avoids frustration, especially for younger players.
